title: Teaching is Work
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Stuart uses a winter-break reflection to attack what he calls one of the most poisonous pieces of non-wisdom in circulation: that if you love what you do you will never work a day in your life. Teachers, he argues, are living proof against it, since they love the job and still come home with aching bones and brains after grading, emailing, calling parents and planning. His first sub-lesson is that teaching's status as real work needs no defending; he has stopped arguing with 'summers off must be nice' remarks, comparing teachers to construction workers while conceding that no generalization covers every individual. The second sub-lesson is a confession: as a new teacher in Baltimore he prided himself on being first in and last out, which he now calls lame. Unlimited hours, he argues, slow a teacher's discovery of which work matters most, so he sets strict hours and does not take work home. He ends by framing teaching as swimming Lake Michigan, refreshing but pulled by an undertow toward complacency and burnout.
points: Stuart targets the maxim that loving your work means never working, arguing that teachers who love the job are the clearest proof that it is still hard labor.
He has stopped defending teachers' workload against 'summers off' jibes, holding that it is as self-evident as the claim that construction workers earn their pay.
His central practical claim is that unlimited hours make a teacher slower, not better, because boundless time delays learning which work is most important.
He models the remedy with fixed working hours of 7:00am to 5:20pm and a no-work-at-home rule, set against his own former workaholism in Baltimore.
His Lake Michigan image casts complacency and burnout as twin undertows, making efficiency against an insane time-to-workload ratio a goal in itself.
quotes: I am nearly positive that, in Hell, there's a book filled with quotes that sound wise but are actually horrifically not so.
Waking up to that alarm on Monday, January 5, is going to be work. Doing the same thing January 6 and every day afterward will be more of the same.

I'm not saying all teachers work hard, just as my uncle in the concrete construction business won't say that all cement guys work hard. Generalizations don't work with individuals, let alone large groups.

Teaching is an excellent way to put bread on the table. I can think of no paid work I'd rather do, especially since I moonlight as a writer for teachers and get paid a bit to do that, too. But becoming a master teacher isn't possible if you give yourself unlimited hours within which to master it for one simple reason: allowing yourself unlimited time to do the work of teaching makes you much slower at figuring out what the most important work of teaching is.

Teaching is like swimming Lake Michigan. It's awesome and it's fresh, and sometimes it's even warm(ish). But there's also this deadly undertow that constantly pulls you into deadly places like Complacency and Burnout.
So many of you have said that one of your greatest struggles in the job is time. I feel that. The time:workload ratio in this job is insane; I want to fight that.
